title: India's Sugar Market Swings From Surplus to Shortage as Prices Hit Record Ahead of Festivals
excerpt: What began as a season of oversupply and falling prices has turned into a scramble to contain record sugar costs, forcing New Delhi to allow imports for the first time in nearly a decade.
body:
• India's sugar prices surged nearly 40% in two months to record highs, reversing a season that began with an 18% production surplus and falling ex-mill prices.
  • New Delhi has banned exports, tightened stockholding limits, and authorized 1 million metric tons of duty-free raw sugar imports — the first in nearly a decade — but traders expect only half that volume to materialize.
  • The government is considering curbing ethanol production from sugarcane juice and B-heavy molasses next season, potentially freeing 3 million metric tons of sugar equivalent for domestic supply.
  • Mill inventories heading into the new season on October 1 are expected to drop to about 3.5 million tons, the lowest in more than three decades, as festival demand peaks.

India started its 2025/26 sugar marketing year in October with a problem most commodity producers envy: too much supply. Production was projected at 30.9 million metric tons, up 18% from the previous year, comfortably exceeding annual domestic demand of roughly 29 million tons. Ex-mill prices in Maharashtra had slid 8-10% from the season's opening levels, hovering around ₹3,600-3,720 per quintal. The government approved 1.5 million tons of exports to drain the glut.

Ten months later, the picture has reversed. Wholesale sugar prices in Kolhapur, a key trading hub in Maharashtra, surged nearly 40% over two months to a record ₹5,350 per 100 kg by mid-August. In Delhi, retail prices have climbed to ₹65-70 per kilogram. Mill inventories heading into the new season on October 1 are expected to fall to about 3.5 million tons — the lowest level in more than three decades.

New Delhi has responded with its most aggressive intervention in years: banning exports, imposing stockholding limits on dealers, and last week authorizing duty-free imports of 1 million metric tons of raw sugar — the first such move in nearly a decade.

How Surplus Became Shortage

Several forces converged to turn surplus into shortage. Patchy monsoon rainfall in Maharashtra and Karnataka, which together account for the bulk of India's sugarcane output, damaged the standing crop and raised concerns about next season's harvest. Mills exported roughly 800,000 tons under the government's earlier quota, drawing down domestic stocks. And ethanol diversion from sugarcane — which consumed about 3 million metric tons of sugar equivalent this season — further tightened available supply.

The ethanol factor is particularly revealing. In September 2025, the government lifted all volume restrictions on ethanol production from sugarcane, eager to hit its 20% fuel-blending target. But oil marketing companies ended up allocating only about 289-307 crore liters from sugar-based feedstocks, favoring grain-based ethanol instead. The mismatch left mills with neither the ethanol revenue they expected nor the sugar stocks to meet demand.

Now the government is considering reversing course: sources told Reuters on August 10 that mills may be barred from producing ethanol from sugarcane juice and B-heavy molasses next season, restricting them to C-heavy molasses, a byproduct with minimal sugar content. The shift could free up roughly 3 million metric tons of sugar equivalent for domestic consumption.

Festival Season Squeeze

India's festival season, running from August through November, drives a predictable demand spike. Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra, and Diwali push consumption of traditional sweets and confectionery higher, and this year, bulk consumers have been building inventories aggressively. The government tightened stockholding limits on August 19, ordering that any bulk consumer using more than 10 metric tons per month can hold no more than 15 days of inventory between September 1 and November 30.

"Consumers and bulk buyers tend to purchase more than they require when they expect prices to rise further, creating additional pressure on demand."

— Vijendra Singh, President, All India Distillers' Association

Not everyone agrees the supply picture is as dire as prices suggest. Singh has argued the rally is driven partly by speculative buying rather than a fundamental shortfall. Fresh supplies from the new crushing season are expected to reach the market by mid-to-late October, roughly 60 days away.

Import Relief May Fall Short

The duty-free import window may also deliver less relief than intended. Domestic ex-mill prices have already fallen about 20% from their peak since the import announcement, eroding margins for potential importers.

"Imports looked attractive last week, when prices were firm and rising. But the sharp price drop since the announcement has taken the shine off imports for millers."

— Rahil Shaikh, Managing Director, MEIR Commodities India

Traders at global houses estimate imports are unlikely to exceed 500,000 tons — half the authorized quota — with most volume taken up by port-based refineries rather than mills. These refineries could quickly sell around 300,000 tons of stocks they already hold into the domestic market, providing some near-term supply relief.

Outlook

The episode underscores how quickly India's sugar market can shift. A year ago, food secretary Sanjeev Chopra was warning that surplus would hurt farmers. Today, the government is scrambling to protect consumers, with measures that carry their own tradeoffs: restricting ethanol production from cane undermines India's biofuel ambitions, while foregone import duties reduce government revenue.

For global markets, the implications are measured. Indian imports of even 500,000 tons would support benchmark prices in London and New York, but the volume is modest by global standards. The larger signal is that India — the world's biggest sugar consumer — remains a swing factor in commodity markets, capable of flipping from exporter to importer within a single season.
author: Diaspora Desk
